summary: Describes the Transaction Key (TKEY) resource record, which can establish shared secret keys between a DNS resolver and server in several modes. Those keys can then secure later DNS messages.

plainLanguage.summary: TKEY lets a DNS resolver and server establish shared secret material for authenticating later DNS messages with TSIG. The record supports several ways to agree on a key and a way to delete one.

questions: how to establish a shared secret with dns
what is the tkey record type number
how does dns diffie-hellman key exchange work
subtitle: A DNS resource record for establishing and deleting shared secret keys between resolvers and servers.

tldr.problem: TSIG can authenticate DNS messages with a shared secret, but does not define how a resolver and server establish that secret except by manual exchange.
tldr.mechanism: A TKEY resource record carries the key-agreement mode and related data in DNS queries and responses. Modes include Diffie-Hellman, GSS-API, assigned keys and key deletion.
tldr.outcome: TKEY supports in-band key establishment for later TSIG use, but the RFC says it does not protect against denial of service. RFC 2930 was updated by RFC 6895.

today: RFC 2930 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2000. It was updated by RFC 6895 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why DNS Needs TKEY
sections.content:
TSIG uses a shared secret to authenticate DNS queries and responses. RFC 2845 does not define a way to set up that secret other than exchanging it manually. RFC 2930 defines the Transaction Key (TKEY) resource record for establishing and deleting shared secrets between a resolver and a server.

TKEY key material is associated with the resolver or server, not with a DNS zone. It can authenticate transactions, but does not provide zone-based data-origin or denial authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: TSIG can check that a DNS message came from someone who knows a shared secret. TKEY defines ways for a resolver and server to establish that secret.

sections.title: Fields in the TKEY Record
sections.content:
TKEY has resource-record type code 249. Its data includes an algorithm name, inception and expiration times, a mode, an error code, key data, and an additional data field reserved for other uses.

TKEY records are meta-records: they are not stored or cached in DNS and do not appear in zone files. Their class SHOULD be 255 (ANY), their TTL SHOULD be zero, and a DNS message must not contain more than one TKEY record. The name identifies the key material; a server returns BADNAME if that name already has different key material.
sections.plainLanguage: A TKEY record carries the method, name and lifetime for key material. DNS does not store or cache the record as ordinary domain data.

sections.title: Modes and DNS Exchanges
sections.content:
The mode field identifies how the key is established or what the TKEY message does. Implementations MUST support Diffie-Hellman key agreement and key deletion; other modes are optional. The additional modes cover GSS-API negotiation and server-assigned or resolver-assigned keying.

In Diffie-Hellman mode, the resolver sends its public key and a nonce in a TKEY query. The server responds with its public key and another nonce. Both sides derive the same secret from the exchanged public keys and nonce data. Other modes carry GSS-API tokens or encrypted key material as specified for that mode.
sections.plainLanguage: In Diffie-Hellman mode, each side sends public information and a nonce. Both sides use those values to calculate the same shared secret without sending that secret in the exchange.

sections.title: Deleting Keys and Managing State
sections.content:
A resolver can ask a server to delete a key by sending an authenticated TKEY deletion request with the key's name. The server MUST implement deletion; it returns BADNAME if it does not know the name. A server may also include a deletion record in a response to tell the resolver that a key is no longer available.

TKEY exchanges require state at both ends. A server that is unwilling to maintain that state must return an error such as NOTIMP or REFUSED, and resolvers may ignore TKEY records they receive.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver can send an authenticated request to remove a named key. Both sides must be willing to keep the state needed to use the key.

sections.title: Authentication and Security Limits
sections.content:
Except in GSS-API mode, TKEY responses MUST be authenticated with a key that was already established. A message must not use the key it is currently trying to provide to prove its own authenticity. TKEY queries also require authentication in the modes specified by the RFC.

The RFC limits the lifetime of a key used to authenticate TKEY messages to prevent old messages from becoming valid again after the time fields wrap. It explicitly states that TKEY does not provide protection against denial-of-service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: A TKEY exchange must be checked with credentials the parties already trust, not with the new key being negotiated. The RFC does not stop an attacker from overwhelming a server with requests.
